messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] DEC Analysis Issues
parts:
Hi Tyler!

So, that tree doesn't have branchlengths.  BioGeoBEARS requires a tree with time branchlengths. (Fossils are OK, e.g. with a tip-dated tree or timescaled with paleotree or some such.).

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#use_dated_phylogenies

Cheers!
Nick

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] DEC Analysis Issues
parts:
Hi -- FigTree gives an error reading that file, so it must have something fundamentally wrong with it.  Looking at it in a text editor, it has some branches of length 0, which will give a BioGeoBEARS error, but you have bigger problems.

You need to walk before you try running, I think.  Your file also doesn't load in the APE package in R, which is crucial as BioGeoBEARS relies on APE to read trees.

So I would say:

1. Get this to work before doing anything else:

In R:
library(ape)
trfn = "timescaleMSM.phy"
tr = read.tree(trfn)
plot(tr)
axisPhylo()

Currently I get this error:

-============
Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : attempt to set index 61/60 in SET_STRING_ELT
=============

As a starting problem, I see 73 "(" characters and 60 ")" characters in the file, but these counts must match exactly for a valid tree specification.


2. Then check that the tree is bifurcating and all branches have positive lengths, and that the tree corresponds to time

3. Only then try additional things like biogeography etc.

Note that there is little point in just tweaking the Newick file so it gets successfully read by APE -- what you really need is a plausibly dated tree that you could publish with, or you are probably just wasting your time.  E.g., your tree has many branch lengths set to 0.5 my, which must be some minimum branch length, but that doesn't seem at all realistic.  The biogeography models *DO* care about the branch lengths, so it really matters whether those branch lengths are some realistic estimate, or just made up.

So, probably, the main strategy is to be patient and spend the time to learn the necessary phylogenetics and dating techniques to get a publishable tree, then come back to the biogeography.

Cheers!
Nick
